\subsection{Recursion categories}

A restriction category with binary restriction products and zeros is
\emph{prodominical} if $f\times0=0$ for every morphism $f$ and every
zero morphism of the required type. It is \emph{isotypical} if any
two of its objects are isomorphic.

A \emph{Turing morphism} on $U$ is a morphism
$\tau:U\times U\rightharpoonup U$ such that, for every object $X$
and every $f:X\times U\rightharpoonup U$, there is a total
parameter morphism $r:X\to U$ satisfying
\[
 f=\tau(r\times1_U).
\]
A \emph{recursion category} here is a prodominical isotypical
category with binary restriction products and a Turing morphism,
as in \cite[Section 9]{Heller}.

A \emph{restriction terminal object} $1$ has a unique total morphism
$!_X:X\to1$ for each object $X$, satisfying
$!_Yf=!_X\bar f$ for every $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$.
A restriction category is \emph{cartesian} if it has binary
restriction products and a restriction terminal object.
A \emph{Turing category} is a cartesian restriction category with an
object $U$, called a \emph{Turing object}, such that every object $X$
admits a total morphism $m_X:X\to U$ and a morphism
$r_X:U\rightharpoonup X$ with $r_Xm_X=1_X$, and there is a
Turing morphism on $U$. This is the characterization of
Cockett--Hofstra~\cite[Theorem 3.4]{CockettHofstra}.

In particular, there is a restriction equivalence
\[
 \Par(\mathcal B_T,\Mono)\simeq\Split(S_T).
\]
Explicitly, a span $C\xleftarrow{m}E\xrightarrow{g}D$ is sent
to $gm^{-1}$, where $m^{-1}$ is the partial inverse just constructed.
Conversely, a partial morphism is represented by its domain
inclusion and its total restriction to that domain. In the predicate
presentation the domain is $\exists y\,G_f(x,y)$; relational
composition identifies composition of these spans by pullback with
composition in $\Split(S_T)$.

The category $\Split(S_T)$ is a Turing category,
with Turing object $U=(\omega,1_\omega)$.
Indeed, the displayed restriction equivalence supplies a restriction
terminal object, represented by the singleton predicate $x=0$.
Binary restriction products are
$(X,e)\times(Y,d)=(X\times Y,e\times d)$.
Every object $(X,e)$ is a retract of $(X,1_X)$, with both morphisms
represented by $e$, and $(X,1_X)\cong U$ by the coding isomorphism.
The Turing morphism extends by the idempotent-splitting argument
of Cockett--Hofstra~\cite[Section 3.5]{CockettHofstra}.
Explicitly, let $\tau:\omega\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$
be the Turing morphism of $S_T$, and let
$f:(X,e)\times U\rightharpoonup U$ be a morphism of $\Split(S_T)$.
Its representative $f:X\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$ in $S_T$
satisfies $f=f(e\times1_\omega)$. Choose a total morphism
$r:X\to\omega$ in $S_T$ with $f=\tau(r\times1_\omega)$.
Then $re:(X,e)\to U$ is total, since $\overline{re}=e$, and
\[
 f=\tau(r\times1_\omega)(e\times1_\omega)
   =\tau((re)\times1_\omega).
\]
The recognition criterion~\cite[Theorem 3.4]{CockettHofstra}
therefore applies.

Ranges extend to $\Split(S_T)$ by the same representatives.
For a morphism $f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$, the equation
$df=f$ implies $\ran_{S_T}(f)\leq d$. This range is therefore
a restriction idempotent on $(Y,d)$, with the same leastness
and agreement properties. Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image}
applies because every monomorphism of $\mathcal B_T$ has a
partial inverse.

The free-variable and substitution algorithms in
Propositions~\ref{prop:st-list-initiality} and
\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization} use these same codes.
Their primitive-recursive traversals therefore give morphisms
\[
 \FV_{\Tm}:\Tm\to W,\quad \FV_{\Fm}:\Fm\to W,\quad
 a_T:\Tm\times(V\times\Tm)\to\Tm,\quad
 b_F:\Fm\times(V\times\Tm)\to1+\Fm
\]
in $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.
For these same codes, Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization}
proves the carrier and constructor equations in $\PA$.
They therefore hold in $\N$. Uniqueness of the parameterized folds
identifies these numerical morphisms with the categorical ones.
In particular,
$\Adm=b_F^{-1}(\Fm\hookrightarrow1+\Fm)$ is the admissibility
subobject, and $a_F:\Adm\to\Fm$ is the induced substitution
morphism. The sentence object is
$j:S\hookrightarrow\Fm$, where
$|S|=\{s\in|\Fm|:\FV_{\Fm}(s)=w_0\}$.

For an endofunctor on the $r$-fold product category $\mathcal D^r$
defined using finite products, coproducts, and specified constant objects, its version on
$(\mathcal D/P)^r$ is obtained
by replacing each constant $X$ by $P\times X\to P$ and using
products and coproducts in that slice. An initial algebra is
\emph{stable under parameters} if, for every $P\in\mathcal D$,
its pullback along $P\to1$ is initial for this slice endofunctor.
For list objects, this is the parameterized recursion property studied by
Cockett~\cite[Lemma 2.2 and Definition 2.3]{CockettLists}.\footnote{The gap
in the printed uniqueness argument for Lemma~5.6 (p.~18) does not affect
Lemma~2.2 or Definition~2.3, cited here.}
Its formulation by pullback into slices is
recalled by Maietti~\cite[Definition 2.4 and the following paragraph]{MaiettiLists}.
